newsitem.title: UK: British Gilts offer short-term rewards.
newsitem.headline: British Gilts offer short-term rewards.

text.p: British government gilts are set to perform well in the short term but will run into trouble in the new year as pressure for an interest rate increase mounts, analysts said on Friday.
"Near term, they're alright, but I'd worry about what the market's going to do in February-March time," said Glenn Davies, chief economist at Credit Lyonnais in London.
Analysts said Britain was in an inflation cycle which would eventually force an interest rate rise, but immediate economic indicators would give support to the gilts market.
"The economics don't look too bad up to the end of the year. The funds situation isn't too bad either," said Davies.

Davies expected the inflation figure for November to show a decline but he forecast a rise in December after increased food prices caused by a French truckers' strike have taken effect. The next retail sales figure would also be soft, he said.

British 10-year gilts showed a spread of 182 basis points against German bunds at 1430 GMT, little changed from the prior close. The spread however, was slightly narrower than the gap between Italian government securities (BTP's) and bunds, which recently has been smaller than the gilt spread.
Analysts said gilts would continue to outperform, helped by a prudent budget from Chancellor Kenneth Clarke, a strong pound and upward momentum in other bond markets.
"Gilts could easily come through 175," said James Barty, chief UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London. "Momentum could well be sustained until the end of the year."

Another boost for the gilt market could come from doubts about European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), particularly over whether a budget stability pact, aiming to ensure countries joining EMU maintain fiscal discipline, would be agreed by EU leaders at a Dublin summit this weekend.
"I think the gilt market might get a bit of a help and be a safe haven," said Davies.
But while gilts are increasingly attractive relative to BTPs and other European bonds, analysts said growing inflationary pressures would weigh increasingly heavily in the medium term.
Barty said gilts were caught in crossfire between the strength of their relative position against BTPs and worries over Britain's cyclical economic position, particularly the rate of economic growth.
"This is going to be an ongoing battle. The outcome of it is probably going to be stalemate until during the course of next year when we'll see bond yields going higher," he said.
Gilts would lose ground in the new year and drift away from the Bund, eroding gains late this year, analysts said.
"We'll be above 200 on the spread going into the election," said Davies.
Britain must hold a general election by May 1997.
Analysts said gilts had also been given a leg-up by sterling's strength which has encouraged an inflow of "hot money" into British securities.
But if these funds were withdrawn, gilts could suffer.

"You're getting money coming in that doesn't have London as its natural habitat," said David Smith, chief economist at Williams de Broe in London. "The danger is that people will start taking profits in the run up to the new year."
Smith said he would not rule out the gilt/Bund spread going to 250 basis points before the election.

The possibility of the opposition Labour party winning the election was a further factor threatening to eat into gilts in the medium term, analysts said. For good or ill, markets still cling to a historical perspective that Labour is a "tax and spend" party, whose policies would not be bond-friendly.
"That's a real negative which has still not been fully priced into the market," said Davies.
